kinds.greenhouse: Greenhouse warming — gases that absorb outgoing longwave radiation
kinds.pollution: Local air pollution — smog, particles and their chemistry near the source
kinds.heat: Direct waste heat — energy released as heat where it is used
kinds.ecosystem: Ecosystem disruption — habitats, water chemistry and ultraviolet exposure
kinds.resource: Resource consumption — water, land and minerals taken from the environment

fossil.q: an average of 9.8 ± 0.5 GtC yr−1 during 2015–2024

luc.q: Global net CO2 emissions from land use averaged 1.4 ± 0.7 GtC yr−1 (5.0 ± 2.6 GtCO2 yr−1) for the 2015–2024 period.

atm.q: The atmospheric CO2 growth rate was 5.6 ± 0.02 GtC yr−1 (2.6 ppm) during the decade 2015–2024 (50 % of total CO2 emissions).

ocean.q: The ocean CO2 sink was 3.2 ± 0.4 GtC yr−1 during the decade 2015–2024

land.q: The land CO2 sink was 2.4 ± 0.8 GtC yr−1 during the 2015–2024 decade but was reduced to 1.9 GtC ± 0.8 GtC yr−1 in 2024.

q: For the year 2024, E FOS increased by 1.1 % relative to 2023, with fossil emissions at 10.3 ± 0.5 GtC yr−1 (including the cement carbonation sink, 0.2 GtC yr−1), E LUC was 1.3 ± 0.7 GtC yr−1, for total anthropogenic CO2 emissions of 11.6 ± 0.9 GtC yr−1 (42.4 ± 3.2 GtCO2 yr−1).

Also, for 2024, G ATM was 7.9 ± 0.2 GtC yr−1 (3.73 ± 0.1 ppm yr−1), 2.2 GtC above the 2023 growth rate. S OCEAN was 3.4 ± 0.4 GtC yr−1 and S LAND was 1.9 ± 1.1 GtC yr−1, leaving a large negative B IM (−1.7 GtC yr−1), suggesting that the total sink or G ATM is strongly overestimated in 2024.

budget.conc: The global atmospheric CO2 concentration averaged over 2024 reached 422.8 ± 0.1 ppm. Preliminary data for 2025 suggest an increase in E FOS relative to 2024 of + 1.0 % (0.2 % to 1.7 %) globally, and atmospheric CO2 concentration increasing by 2.1 ppm reaching 425.6 ppm, 53 % above the pre-industrial level (around 278 ppm in 1750).
defs: Fossil CO2 emissions (E FOS) are based on energy and cement production data. Emissions from land-use change (E LUC) are estimated by bookkeeping models based on land-use data. The global atmospheric CO2 growth rate (G ATM) is computed from changes in concentration measured at surface stations.
The sum of all sources and sinks results in the carbon budget imbalance (B IM), a measure of imperfect data and incomplete understanding of the contemporary carbon cycle.
shares: The ocean sink ... has taken up 29 % of the total emissions in the past decade
The land sink, which is the global net uptake of CO2 by the land excluding land use, has taken up 21 % of the total emissions in the past decade
feedback: The effects of climate change and climate variability act to reduce the land and ocean CO2 sinks by 25 % and 7.1 % respectively, on average for the 2015–2024 period.
The ocean sink is negatively affected by altered oceanic circulation and surface warming which decreases CO2 solubility.
history: Total anthropogenic emissions more than doubled since the 1960s, from 4.9 ± 0.7 GtC yr−1 for the decade of the 1960s to an average of 11.2 ± 0.9 GtC yr−1 during 2015–2024
Cumulative anthropogenic CO2 emissions (fossil, including cement carbonation, and land-use change) for 1850–2024 totalled 745 ± 65 GtC (2730 ± 240 GtCO2)
During the historical period 1850–2024, 67 % of historical emissions were from fossil emissions and 33 % from land-use change.
budget.disagreement: GCB 2025 gives the 2024 land sink as 1.9 ± 1.1 GtC yr−1 in its abstract and 1.9 ± 0.8 in its key messages.
budget.preprint: A “Global Carbon Budget 2026” exists only as a preprint under review (ESSD Discussions, 10 Nov 2026); not used.

sectors.total: According to the latest data, global GHG emissions in 2025 reached 54.1 Gt CO2eq (without Land Use, land Use Change and Forestry). The 2025 data experienced an increase of 0.7% or 380 Mt CO2eq compared to the levels in 2024.
sectors.gases: In 2025, the majority of GHG emissions consisted of fossil CO2 accounting for 73.8% of total emissions, while CH4 contributed for 17.6% to the total, N2O for 5.3% and F-gases for 3.3%.
sectors.power: Compared to 2024, emissions increased across all sectors, with the exception of the power sector which saw a slight decrease of emissions (-51.0 Mt CO2eq or -0.3%), keeping however, the role of dominant sector with a share of nearly 30% in global GHG emissions.
sectors.gwp: aggregated using Global Warming Potential values from IPCC AR5 (GWP-100 AR5)

rows.name: Power industry
rows.def: Power industry includes power and heat generation plants (public and auto-producers).

rows.name: Agriculture
rows.def: Agriculture includes agriculture livestock (enteric fermentation, manure management), agriculture soils (fertilisers, lime application, rice cultivation, direct soil emissions, indirect N2O emissions from agriculture), field burning of agricultural residues.

rows.name: Industrial combustion
rows.def: Industrial combustion and processes include combustion for industrial manufacturing and industrial process emissions (e.g. non-metallic minerals, non-ferrous metals, solvents and other product use, chemicals, etc.)

rows.name: Fuel production
rows.def: fuel extraction, transformation and refineries activities, including venting and flaring.

sectors.licenceNote: Report text is EU-owned (CC BY 4.0); the fossil-CO2 part of the sector data comes from IEA (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0), so sector values are shown as read, not redistributed as a file.

methane.latest: Global CH4 Monthly Means August 2026: 1936.37 ppb August 2025: 1931.29 ppb
methane.method: The graphs show globally-averaged, monthly mean atmospheric methane abundance determined from marine surface sites.
methane.meaning: It represents the sum of all CH4 added to, and removed from, the atmosphere during the year by human activities and natural processes.
methane.caveat: the initial, April estimate of the annual increase is likely to change significantly as more data are added
methane.rise: CH4 is the second most important human-influenced greenhouse gas in terms of climate forcing after carbon dioxide (CO2), and both emissions and atmospheric concentrations of CH4 have continued to increase since 2007 after a temporary pause.
methane.topdown: For the 2010–2019 decade, global CH4 emissions are estimated by atmospheric inversions (top-down) to be 575 Tg CH4 yr−1 (range 553–586, corresponding to the minimum and maximum estimates of the model ensemble). Of this amount, 369 Tg CH4 yr−1 or ∼ 65 % is attributed to direct anthropogenic sources in the fossil, agriculture, and waste and anthropogenic biomass burning (range 350–391 Tg CH4 yr−1 or 63 %–68 %).
methane.bottomup: Bottom-up methods suggest 16 % (94 Tg CH4 yr−1) larger global emissions (669 Tg CH4 yr−1, range 512–849) than top-down inversion methods for the 2010–2019 period.
methane.y2020: The 2020 emission rate is the highest of the period and reaches 608 Tg CH4 yr−1 (range 581–627), which is 12 % higher than the average emissions in the 2000s.
methane.wetlands: Bottom-up approaches show that the combined wetland and inland freshwater emissions average 248 [159–369] Tg CH4 yr−1 for the 2010–2019 decade.
methane.sinks: The total sink of CH4 is estimated at 633 [507–796] Tg CH4 yr−1 by the bottom-up approaches and at 554 [550–567] Tg CH4 yr−1 by top-down approaches.
livestock: Of these activities, globally and in most countries, livestock is by far the largest source of CH4, followed by waste handling and rice cultivation.
Enteric domestic ruminants such as cattle, buffalo, sheep, goats, and camels emit CH4 as a by-product of the anaerobic microbial activity in their digestive systems
There are currently (2020) about 1.5 billion cattle globally, almost 1.3 billion sheep, and nearly as many goats

land.q: Emissions from deforestation, the main driver of global gross emissions, remain high at around 1.9 GtC yr−1 over the 2015–2024 period, highlighting the strong potential of halting deforestation for emissions reductions. Sequestration of 1.3 GtC yr−1 through re-/afforestation and forest regrowth in shifting cultivation cycles offsets two third of the deforestation emissions. In addition, smaller net emissions are due to wood harvest and forest management, peat drainage and peat fire.
land.caution: The NGHGI data under the land-use, land-use change, and forestry (LULUCF) sector ... and the LULUCF estimates from FAOSTAT ... differ from the global models' definition of E LUC

aviation.growth: Aviation grew strongly over the past decades (1960–2018) in terms of activity, with revenue passenger kilometers increasing from 109 to 8269 billion km yr−1, and in terms of climate change impacts, with CO2 emissions increasing by a factor of 6.8–1034 Tg CO2 yr−1.
aviation.erf: For 2018 the net aviation ERF is +100.9 mW (mW) m−2 (5–95% likelihood range of (55, 145)) with major contributions from contrail cirrus (57.4 mW m−2), CO2 (34.3 mW m−2), and NOx (17.5 mW m−2). Non-CO2 terms sum to yield a net positive (warming) ERF that accounts for more than half (66%) of the aviation net ERF in 2018.
aviation.share: Using normalization to aviation fuel use, the contribution of global aviation in 2011 was calculated to be 3.5 (4.0, 3.4) % of the net anthropogenic ERF of 2290 (1130, 3330) mW m−2.
aviation.contrails: Contrail cirrus, consisting of linear contrails and the cirrus cloudiness arising from them, yields the largest positive net (warming) ERF term followed by CO2 and NOx emissions. The formation and emission of sulfate aerosol yields a negative (cooling) term. The mean contrail cirrus ERF/RF ratio of 0.42 indicates that contrail cirrus is less effective in surface warming than other terms.
aviation.plain: contrails and contrail cirrus – short-lived clouds created in jet engine exhaust plumes at aircraft cruise altitudes that reflect sunlight during the day and trap heat trying to escape at night.
aviation.uncertainty: Uncertainty distributions (5%, 95%) show that non-CO2 forcing terms contribute about 8 times more than CO2 to the uncertainty in the aviation net ERF in 2018.
aviation.erfDef: ERF represents the increase or decrease in the balance between the energy coming from the sun and the energy emitted from the Earth since pre-industrial times.
aviation.note: The terms printed do not add to the net: the sulfate (cooling) and other smaller terms make up the difference (abstract only; the full paper was not readable).

cement.third: Global production of cement has grown very rapidly in recent years, and, after fossil fuels and land-use change, it is the third-largest source of anthropogenic emissions of carbon dioxide.
cement.total: Global process emissions in 2018 were 1.50±0.12 Gt CO2, equivalent to about 4 % of emissions from fossil fuels. Cumulative emissions from 1928 to 2018 were 38.3±2.4 Gt CO2, 71 % of which have occurred since 1990.
cement.chem: There are two aspects of cement production that result in emissions of CO2. First is the chemical reaction involved in the production of the main component of cement, clinker, as carbonates (largely CaCO3, found in limestone) are decomposed into oxides (largely lime, CaO) and CO2 by the addition of heat.
cement.eq: where Mr CO2 is the molecular weight of CO2, Mr CaO the molecular weight of CaO, f clink CaO the fraction of CaO in clinker, f cem clink the fraction of clinker in cement (the "clinker ratio"), and M cem the mass of cement
cement.energy: The second source of emissions is from the combustion of fossil fuels to generate the significant energy required to heat the raw ingredients to well over 1000 °C, and these "energy" emissions, including those from purchased electricity, could add a further 60 % on top of the process emissions (IEA, 2016). Total emissions from the cement industry could therefore contribute as much as 8 % of global CO2 emissions.

caoClinker.q: In the earlier 1996 IPCC Guidelines, the information sourced from CDIAC stated that the average CaO content of cement is 0.635, while the CaO content of clinker is 0.646, yielding an implicit average clinker ratio of cement of 0.98.

ipccEF.q: Indian analyses have shown emission factors (t CO2 (t clinker)−1) similar to the default IPCC factor of 0.52 (Arceivala, 2014), so I use that factor here.

ratio.q: The global-average clinker ratio has declined from approximately 0.83 in 1990 to 0.67 in 2013 (Fig. A1) – consistent with an estimate of 0.65 made by the IEA (2017) – before rebounding to 0.71 in 2018

carbonation.q: from an average of 20 MtC yr−1 (0.02 GtC yr−1) in the 1960s to an average of 210 MtC yr−1 (0.21 GtC yr−1) during 2015–2024

cement.older: Andrew also quotes an older estimate that process emissions “contribute about 5 % of total anthropogenic CO2 emissions excluding land-use change (Boden et al., 2017)” — different from his own “about 4 % of emissions from fossil fuels” for 2018.

lca.method: NREL considered approximately 3,000 published life cycle assessment studies on utility-scale electricity generation ... Less than 15% of the original pool of references passed this review process.
lca.phases: For fossil-fueled technologies, fuel combustion during operation of the facility emits the vast majority of GHGs. For nuclear and renewable energy technologies, most GHG emissions occur upstream of operation.
lca.cradle: Life cycle assessments (LCA) can help quantify environmental burdens from "cradle to grave" and facilitate more-consistent comparisons of energy technologies.
lca.coal20: from cradle to grave, coal-fired electricity releases about 20 times more GHGs per kilowatt-hour than solar, wind, or nuclear electricity (based on median estimates for each technology).
lca.median: the sum of the median estimates of each life cycle phase for a given generation technology might not equal the median of the total life cycle emissions factors (the sum of the medians need not equal the median of the sums).
lca.storage: we considered only references that enabled the calculation of emissions per unit of electricity delivered over the lifetime of the storage system.
lca.units: All values are in grams of carbon dioxide equivalent per kilowatt-hour (g CO2e/kWh)
lca.ranges: The fact sheet prints minimum and maximum only on a chart (Figure 2); numeric ranges are in the NLR data catalogue, which was offline on 2026-11-28 — so only medians are shown here.
lca.renamed: NREL has since been renamed the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR).

heat.q: human primary energy consumption amounted to 595 EJ in 2021 (BP, 2022), which translates into an average heat release of 18.9 TW. When averaged over land, this yields 18.9 TW / (29 % × 510 × 10^12 m^2) = 0.13 W m−2 (as in Jin et al., 2019), while globally, this yields 0.04 W m−2 when evenly distributed over the Earth's surface. This heat release is minute compared to the downwelling flux of longwave radiation of 346 W m−2 (Stephens et al., 2012) and the observed radiative forcing change at the top of the atmosphere of 2.7 W m−2 that can clearly be attributed to the increase in greenhouse gases (Forster et al., 2021).
heat.local: it is also well known and established that anthropogenic heat emissions can affect local climate (e.g., Block et al., 2004; Forster et al., 2007), especially in urban and highly populated areas, resulting in the urban heat island effect.
heat.models: Studies that incorporated this effect in climate models showed little, if any, effect on global climate (Flanner, 2009), consistent with the energy balance estimate described earlier.
heat.label: An editorial in Earth System Dynamics (2023) — energy-balance arithmetic, not a new research result.

uhi.q: A review of research studies and data found that in the United States, the heat island effect results in daytime temperatures in urban areas about 1–7°F higher than temperatures in outlying areas and nighttime temperatures about 2–5°F higher. Humid regions (primarily in the eastern United States) and cities with larger and denser populations experience the greatest temperature differences.
uhi.mech: Structures such as buildings, roads, and other infrastructure absorb and re-emit the sun's heat more than natural landscapes such as forests and water bodies.
causes: Trees, vegetation, and water bodies tend to cool the air by providing shade, transpiring water from plant leaves, and evaporating surface water, respectively.
Often, heat islands build throughout the day and become more pronounced after sunset due to the slow release of heat from urban materials.
Cities with many narrow streets and tall buildings become urban canyons, which can block natural wind flow that would bring cooling effects.

Vehicles, air-conditioning units, buildings, and industrial facilities all emit heat into the urban environment. These sources of human-generated, or anthropogenic, waste heat can contribute to heat island effects.
Calm and clear weather conditions result in more severe heat islands ... Conversely, strong winds and cloud cover suppress heat island formation.
uhi.roof: On a warm day, conventional roofing materials may reach as much as 66°F warmer than the surrounding air temperatures.
uhi.ac: Increased electricity demand for air conditioning ranges from 1–9% for each 2°F increase in temperature, with the highest increase in countries where most buildings have air conditioning, such as the United States.
uhi.ozone: Ground-level ozone, in particular, is formed when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in the presence of sunlight and hot weather.

water.total: Water use in the United States in 2015 was estimated to be about 322 billion gallons per day (Bgal/d), which was 9 percent less than in 2010. The 2015 estimates put total withdrawals at the lowest level since before 1970
water.thermo: Thermoelectric-power withdrawals accounted for 41 percent of total withdrawals for all uses, and freshwater withdrawals for thermoelectric power accounted for 34 percent of the total freshwater withdrawals for all uses. Total consumptive use for thermoelectric power was 4.31 Bgal/d in 2015 or 3 percent of the total thermoelectric-power withdrawals.
water.irrigation: Total consumptive use for irrigation was 73.2 Bgal/d in 2015 or 62 percent of the total use (withdrawals and reclaimed wastewater).
water.note: Withdrawn is not the same as consumed: most cooling water goes back to the river or lake — warmer.

ozone.credit: World Meteorological Organization (WMO), Executive Summary. Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion: 2026, GAW Report No. 327, 55 pp., WMO, Geneva, Switzerland, 2026.
ozone.recovering: The atmospheric abundances of chlorine and bromine contained in controlled ozone-depleting substances (ODSs) continue to decrease because of the actions taken under the Montreal Protocol. As a consequence, clear signs that the stratospheric ozone layer is beginning to recover have emerged.
ozone.dates: In a middle-of-the-road greenhouse-gas scenario, Antarctic TCO is projected to return to 1980 values during the 2060s. ... Near-global-mean TCO is projected to return to 1980 values around 2040. Altogether, the findings show that the Montreal Protocol is working well and is expected to meet its goals and those of the Vienna Convention provided there is continued compliance.
ozone.arctic: it has become clearer that the concept of the date of return to 1980 levels is not appropriate for this region. In contrast to previous Assessments, a projected Arctic return date is not highlighted in this Executive Summary.
ozone.def: Return dates are defined as the return of decadally smoothed TCO time series to a historical benchmark.
ozone.cooling: The mid-to-upper stratosphere has cooled globally by about 0.5 °C decade–1 from 1979 to 2024. This cooling is primarily because of continued increases in carbon dioxide (CO2) abundances.
ozone.emerging: Emerging technologies such as a hydrogen economy, rocket launches/space debris, and supersonic aviation have so far had only minor effects on stratospheric ozone depletion compared to those from ODSs.
ozone.prev: TCO is expected to return to 1980 values around 2066 in the Antarctic, around 2045 in the Arctic, and around 2040 for the near-global average (60°N-60°S).
ozone.citeNote: The Executive Summary page’s own citation box prints “2022” for this GAW Report No. 327; the 2026 introduction page and the report number show it is the 2026 assessment.

removal.what: Direct air capture technology is a form of carbon dioxide (CO2) removal that takes CO2 from ambient, or still, air. The separated CO2 can then be permanently stored deep underground, or it can be converted into products.
how: Solvent-based direct air capture systems pass air through chemicals that remove the CO2. Existing systems use a combination of heat and vacuum to remove the captured CO2 and return the chemicals to the direct air capture process.

Sorbent-based direct air capture systems use physical filters. These filters chemically bind with CO2 molecules. When the filters are heated and/or placed under a vacuum, they release the CO2, which is now in a concentrated stream.
removal.energy: The downside to direct air capture is its current cost. Removing CO2 from the air takes lots of power because only a tiny percentage of the atmosphere is made up of CO2. The technology also involves costs to store or use the captured CO2.
removal.goal: DOE launched the Carbon Negative Shot initiative—a call for innovation in carbon dioxide removal pathways that will capture CO2 from the atmosphere and store it at 1 billion ton scales for less than $100 per net metric ton of CO2-equivalent.
removal.tradeoff: For example, technologies like DAC currently require substantial infrastructure investments and energy inputs but are highly measurable and verifiable. In contrast, approaches such as improved forest management leverage the photosynthetic productivity of natural and working ecosystems but can be challenging to measure at high spatial and temporal resolution and provide less durable storage.
removal.scale: the atmosphere-to-geosphere flux of carbon resulting from carbon dioxide removal (CDR) activities in 2024 is estimated at 0.011 MtC yr−1. This results primarily from 0.0048 MtC yr−1 of biomass direct storage (compressing waste biomass to store underground), 0.003 and 0.002 MtC yr−1 of mineralisation and enhanced weathering projects respectively, and 0.0004 MtC yr−1 of DACCS (Pongratz et al., 2024). ... although it remains roughly a million times smaller than current fossil CO2 emissions.
removal.shortfall: the lower DACCS estimate ... reflect[s] updated CDR tracking methodologies which include drawing on more accurate annual data from registries, indicating that operational projects are currently removing less CO2 than their expected capacities.
removal.gap: No openly citable number for the energy needed per tonne captured was found in an allowed source, so none is shown.

srm.disclaimer: Importantly, the issuance of this report does not signal any Executive Branch policy decision(s) regarding SRM. The report is only a response to Congressional directive.
srm.mech: greenhouse gases warm the climate by blocking a portion of outgoing longwave radiation that would otherwise be emitted into space. By contrast, SRM cools the climate by reflecting a greater amount of incoming solar (shortwave) radiation back into space. Because these are different physical mechanisms, an environment with SRM would be different from any without it.
limits: SRM would not ameliorate most of the impacts of ocean acidification, which is primarily driven by rising atmospheric carbon dioxide levels, nor eliminate the tendency for fossil fuel burning to worsen air quality.
SRM might halt but would not result in the rapid reversal of some important manifestations of climate warming, such as loss of land ice and greenhouse gas emissions from thawing permafrost.
Stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI), for example, can alter stratospheric heating, circulation, and chemistry (including accelerating ozone depletion)
deployment of SRM would inevitably involve its own risks, almost all of which are poorly understood and some of which are unknown.
srm.termination: assess the risks associated with sudden termination of SRM.
ozone: Choosing a middle-of-the-road greenhouse-gas scenario and assuming an injected sulfate aerosol mass sufficient to stabilize global warming, global ozone depletion becomes 3–5 DU at mid-century, which delays the recovery of global TCO by around 15-20 years.
Models simulate decreases in Antarctic October TCO due to SAI ranging from 17 to 37 DU, corresponding to a delay in recovery of about 10–15 years.
srm.assumptions: The simulations use a middle-of-the-road climate scenario (SSP2-4.5) and the WMO (2014) ODS scenario. Sulfate-based SAI is carried out from 2035 onwards with progressively increasing SO2 injection rates in the subtropics of both hemispheres
srm.strategy: Climate model simulations show that the magnitude, and in some regions the sign, of the stratospheric ozone response to SAI depends strongly on the strategy, including the latitude of injection and the injected material.
srm.lowconf: Overall confidence in the effects of non-sulfate SAI materials on stratospheric ozone remains low due to limited data on their physicochemical properties under stratospheric conditions.
srm.volcano: SAI, proposes to intentionally enhance stratospheric aerosol loading to reflect more incoming solar radiation back to space, similar to the natural effects from large volcanic eruptions.
srm.scope: This Research Plan does not consider space-based approaches to SRM

mining.what: Mine drainage refers to any surface water or groundwater that drains from an active or abandoned mining operation. Mine drainage can be high-quality similar to natural waters or contaminated by leftover materials. Polluted mine drainage can be extremely acidic and is often laden with high concentrations of toxic, heavy metals. In general, the more acidic the water, the more likely it is to be harmful to living organisms.
mining.mech: Mine drainage forms from a chemical reaction between water and rocks containing sulfur-bearing minerals. The resulting waters become rich in sulfuric acid and dissolved iron. As the iron settles out of the water, it can form red, orange, or yellow sediments in the bottom of streams. The acidic runoff further dissolves heavy metals such as copper, lead, mercury into groundwater or surface water. The rate and degree by which acid-mine drainage proceeds can be increased by the action of certain bacteria.
mining.event: On August 5, 2015, U.S. EPA was conducting an investigation of the Gold King Mine near Silverton, Colorado. While excavating as part of the investigation, water began leaking from the mine tunnel, and about three million gallons of water and sediment were released into Cement Creek, a tributary of the Animas River.
mining.water: Total mining withdrawals in 2015 were 4.00 Bgal/d
